### Problem: Video Stitching {#sec-int-p4-c}

::: {.p-statement}
A sporting event lasted `time` seconds. You have $n$ video clips; clip $i$ covers $[s_i, e_i]$ and may be cut into pieces freely ($1 \le n \le 100$, $0 \le s_i \le e_i \le 100$, $1 \le \texttt{time} \le 100$). Return the **minimum number of clips** whose pieces cover the whole event $[0, \texttt{time}]$, or $-1$ if it cannot be covered.

Source: [LC 1024 · Video Stitching](https://leetcode.com/problems/video-stitching/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}

Example: `clips = [[0,2],[4,6],[8,10],[1,9],[1,5],[5,9]]`, `time = 10` → $3$ (take $[0,2]$, $[1,9]$, $[8,10]$). With `clips = [[0,1],[1,2]]` and `time = 5` the answer is $-1$.
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Grow a covered prefix $[0, \text{reach}]$ one clip at a time. Every clip that starts inside the prefix could be the next one, and the best of them is simply the one that **ends farthest**: whatever an optimal answer does next, replacing its next clip by the farthest-reaching one leaves at least as much covered. If no clip that starts inside the prefix reaches past it, there is a hole and the answer is $-1$. This is covering, the third greedy of @sec-int-sched, and it is the jump game of @sec-od-p4-jump2 in interval clothes.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Try subsets by size.** For $r = 1, 2, \dots$, test every $r$-subset with a sort-and-walk coverage check; the first $r$ that covers $[0, \texttt{time}]$ is the answer. Exponential; the oracle.
2. **Sort by start, extend to the farthest end.** Sort by start. Repeatedly scan the clips with $s \le \text{reach}$, take the largest end among them as the new `reach`, and count one clip. Stop with $-1$ when `reach` cannot grow. $O(n\log n)$.
3. **Bucket by start, then layers.** Since starts are at most $100$, store `far[s]`, the largest end of a clip starting at $s$, and replace the sort by a scan of positions $0..\texttt{time}-1$, exactly the layer walk of Jump Game II. $O(n + \texttt{time})$.

**Invariant.** After $c$ clips the greedy's `reach` is the largest prefix $[0, \text{reach}]$ that any $c$ clips can cover ("greedy stays ahead"). Proof by induction: the $(c+1)$-th clip of any solution must start inside the prefix that its first $c$ clips cover, which is no longer than the greedy's, so it is one of the clips the greedy considered, and the greedy took the farthest one.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Try subsets by size

::: {.form-next}
The definition. A chosen set covers $[0, \texttt{time}]$ when, sorted by start, each clip starts at or before the point covered so far, the first one starts at $0$, and the walk reaches `time`. Trying sizes $1, 2, \dots$ makes the first success a minimum. $O(2^n \cdot n\log n)$; tiny inputs only.

**Worked example.** On the sample, no single clip covers $[0,10]$ and no pair does either (only $[0,2]$ starts at $0$, and no clip covers $[2,10]$); the triple $[0,2],[1,9],[8,10]$ does. Answer $3$.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def covers(chosen, time):
    reach = 0                                   # [0, reach] is covered
    for s, e in sorted(chosen):
        if s > reach:
            break                               # a hole at (reach, s)
        reach = max(reach, e)
    return reach >= time


def stitch_brute(clips, time):
    for r in range(1, len(clips) + 1):
        for combo in itertools.combinations(clips, r):
            if covers(combo, time):
                return r
    return -1
```

##### C++

```cpp
// fragment - exponential oracle
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;
int stitchBrute(const vector<vector<int>>& clips, int time) {
    int n = (int)clips.size(), best = -1;
    for (int mask = 1; mask < (1 << n); ++mask) {
        vector<vector<int>> c;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) if (mask >> i & 1) c.push_back(clips[i]);
        sort(c.begin(), c.end());
        int reach = 0;
        for (auto& x : c) { if (x[0] > reach) break; reach = max(reach, x[1]); }
        int k = __builtin_popcount(mask);
        if (reach >= time && (best == -1 || k < best)) best = k;
    }
    return best;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `covers` is the merge walk of @sec-int-merge stopped at the first gap: with `reach` as the end of the covered prefix, a clip starting after `reach` proves that the point just after `reach` is missing. Starting `reach` at $0$ encodes "the cover must begin at $0$": a clip starting at $1$ is already a hole. Clips are closed, so a clip starting exactly at `reach` continues the cover.

#### Sort by start, extend to the farthest end

::: {.form-next}
Instead of trying subsets, choose the next clip: among all clips that start inside $[0, \text{reach}]$, the one with the farthest end. Sort by start once; a single pointer then walks the clips, because a clip that becomes usable stays usable as `reach` grows. Each round costs one clip; a round that cannot grow `reach` means a hole. $O(n\log n)$ time, $O(1)$ extra state.

**Worked example.** Sorted: $[0,2],[1,5],[1,9],[4,6],[5,9],[8,10]$. Round 1: clips starting at $\le 0$: $[0,2]$, so `reach = 2`. Round 2: starts $\le 2$: $[1,5],[1,9]$, farthest $9$, `reach = 9`. Round 3: starts $\le 9$: $[4,6],[5,9],[8,10]$, farthest $10$, `reach = 10` $\ge$ `time`. Three clips.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-1024-greedy
def stitch_greedy(clips, time):
    clips = sorted(clips)
    i, n = 0, len(clips)
    reach, count = 0, 0
    while reach < time:
        best = reach
        while i < n and clips[i][0] <= reach:       # every clip usable now
            best = max(best, clips[i][1])
            i += 1
        if best == reach:                           # nothing extends the cover: a hole
            return -1
        reach, count = best, count + 1
    return count

for _ in range(300):
    time = random.randint(1, 10)
    clips = []
    for _ in range(random.randint(1, 7)):
        s = random.randint(0, 10)
        clips.append([s, min(10, s + random.randint(0, 5))])
    assert stitch_greedy(clips, time) == stitch_brute(clips, time)
assert stitch_greedy([[0, 2], [4, 6], [8, 10], [1, 9], [1, 5], [5, 9]], 10) == 3
assert stitch_greedy([[0, 1], [1, 2]], 5) == -1
assert stitch_greedy([[0, 4], [2, 8]], 5) == 2
print("stitch_greedy OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;
int videoStitching(vector<vector<int>>& clips, int time) {
    sort(clips.begin(), clips.end());
    int i = 0, n = (int)clips.size(), reach = 0, count = 0;
    while (reach < time) {
        int best = reach;
        while (i < n && clips[i][0] <= reach) best = max(best, clips[i++][1]);
        if (best == reach) return -1;              // a hole right after reach
        reach = best; ++count;
    }
    return count;
}

int main() {
    vector<vector<int>> c{{0,2},{4,6},{8,10},{1,9},{1,5},{5,9}};
    return videoStitching(c, 10) == 3 ? 0 : 1;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** The inner loop never rewinds: clips are sorted by start and `reach` only grows, so each clip is examined once over the whole run, and the cost after sorting is $O(n)$. The hole test `best == reach` is exact: if no usable clip ends after `reach`, then no clip at all covers the points just after `reach` (any clip covering them either starts inside the prefix, and was usable, or starts after `reach`). This is the merge walk once more, with a different decision at each step: merging keeps *every* interval, covering keeps *one per round*.

#### Bucket by start, then layers

::: {.form-next}
The starts are small integers, so the sort can go. Store `far[s]` = the largest end of a clip starting at $s$. Walk the positions $x = 0, 1, \dots, \texttt{time} - 1$ while keeping `nxt`, the farthest end among clips starting at or before $x$. When $x$ reaches the end of the current cover, one more clip is needed, and the cover jumps to `nxt`. This is Jump Game II's layer scan (@sec-od-p4-jump2) with `far[x]` in place of `x + nums[x]`. $O(n + \texttt{time})$.

**Worked example.** `far` $= [2, 9, 0, 0, 6, 9, 0, 0, 10, 0, 0]$. $x = 0$: `nxt = 2`; the cover ends at $0$, so count $1$, cover $= 2$. $x = 1, 2$: `nxt = 9`; at $x = 2$ count $2$, cover $= 9$. $x = 3..9$: `nxt = 10`; at $x = 9$ count $3$, cover $= 10 \ge 10$. Answer $3$.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-1024-layers
def stitch_layers(clips, time):
    far = [0] * (time + 1)
    for s, e in clips:
        if s <= time:
            far[s] = max(far[s], e)
    count, cover, nxt = 0, 0, 0                 # [0, cover] is covered by `count` clips
    for x in range(time):
        nxt = max(nxt, far[x])
        if x == cover:                          # the current cover is used up at x
            if nxt <= x:
                return -1                       # nothing reaches past x: a hole
            count, cover = count + 1, nxt
            if cover >= time:
                return count
    return count if cover >= time else -1

for _ in range(300):
    time = random.randint(1, 10)
    clips = []
    for _ in range(random.randint(1, 7)):
        s = random.randint(0, 10)
        clips.append([s, min(10, s + random.randint(0, 5))])
    assert stitch_layers(clips, time) == stitch_brute(clips, time)
assert stitch_layers([[0, 2], [4, 6], [8, 10], [1, 9], [1, 5], [5, 9]], 10) == 3
assert stitch_layers([[0, 1], [1, 2]], 5) == -1
print("stitch_layers OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;
int videoStitchingLayers(const vector<vector<int>>& clips, int time) {
    vector<int> far(time + 1, 0);
    for (auto& c : clips) if (c[0] <= time) far[c[0]] = max(far[c[0]], c[1]);
    int count = 0, cover = 0, nxt = 0;
    for (int x = 0; x < time; ++x) {
        nxt = max(nxt, far[x]);
        if (x == cover) {
            if (nxt <= x) return -1;
            ++count; cover = nxt;
            if (cover >= time) return count;
        }
    }
    return cover >= time ? count : -1;
}

int main() {
    vector<vector<int>> c{{0,2},{4,6},{8,10},{1,9},{1,5},{5,9}};
    return videoStitchingLayers(c, 10) == 3 ? 0 : 1;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** Clips starting after `time` are useless and are dropped when building `far`. The loop runs over positions *strictly below* `time` because a clip must start before `time` to add anything to the cover. At the moment `x == cover`, the clips started so far are exactly the usable ones of form 2's round, and `nxt` is their farthest end, so the two forms make the same choice of reach in each round; only the bookkeeping changed.
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Try subsets by size** is $O(2^n \cdot n\log n)$ time and $O(n)$ space. **Sort by start, extend to the farthest end** is $O(n\log n)$ time and $O(1)$ extra space. **Bucket by start, then layers** is $O(n + \texttt{time})$ time and $O(\texttt{time})$ space, which only makes sense because the coordinates are at most $100$.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- **No clip starts at $0$**: the first round finds nothing usable and returns $-1$.
- **A hole in the middle** (`[[0,1],[2,5]]`, `time = 5`): the second round cannot grow `reach` past $1$; $-1$.
- **Clips that run past `time`** (`[[0,20]]`, `time = 5`): one clip; the loop stops as soon as `reach >= time`.
- **Touching clips** $[0,2],[2,5]$: closed ends, so $2$ clips cover $[0,5]$; the test `s <= reach` accepts a clip that starts exactly at the covered end.
- **Zero-length clips** $[3,3]$: never extend anything; harmless.
:::

- [CF 1066B · Heaters](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1066/B){rating="1500"} — cover every position of an array with the fewest heaters of radius $r$: the same farthest-reach greedy, where each heater is an interval $[i - r + 1, i + r - 1]$.
- [LC 1326 · Minimum Number of Taps to Open to Water a Garden](https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-number-of-taps-to-open-to-water-a-garden/){difficulty="Hard"} — tap $i$ waters $[i - r_i, i + r_i]$; turn the taps into intervals and run this problem.
